body:
An escaped quote inside a `$( )` substitution desynchronises the word scanner in `lib/bash-write-guard.ts`, the redirect operator is swallowed with the rest of the word, and the write is ALLOWed. **Executed: the file was overwritten.**

The substitution scanner skips quoted spans with `indexOf`:

```ts
const q = s[j];
if (q === "'" || q === '"') {
  const close = s.indexOf(q, j + 1);
  j = close === -1 ? s.length : close;
  continue;
}
```

`indexOf` cannot tell `"` from `\"`, so inside a double-quoted span the escaped quote is read as the closing one.

## Measured, with controls, on `origin/main`

`decideBashWrite()` against a protected basename:

| spelling | decision |
|---|---|
| `echo hi > <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| `chmod 777 <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| `echo $(echo "x)") > <protected>` | BLOCK (control — the paren-in-string case, already fixed) |
| `echo $(echo 'x)') > <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| `echo \$(echo x) > <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| **`echo $(echo "x\"") > <protected>`** | **ALLOW** |
| **`echo $(echo "a\")b") > <protected>`** | **ALLOW** |

Five blocking controls, so this is a reading and not a dead instrument.

## And they run

The whole argument for treating the unterminated spellings as acceptable is that they are not valid bash. That defence does not reach these two. Executed against a real file seeded with `ORIGINAL`:

```
  *** WROTE   rc=0  plain redirect (control)   victim now: hi
  *** WROTE   rc=0  escaped dq in $()          victim now: x\"
  *** WROTE   rc=0  escaped dq then paren      victim now: a\"\)b
  INERT       rc=2  unterminated dq            bash: unexpected EOF
  INERT       rc=2  unterminated $(            bash: unexpected EOF
```

Two of the four ALLOWed spellings are valid bash that exits 0 and overwrites the target. The other two are syntax errors and are genuinely inert — **that half of the automated review's finding does not hold, and I am not asking for it to be fixed.**

## Not introduced by #1213, and it should not block it

I ran the identical battery against #1213's head (`origin/pr-1213`) and against `origin/main`. Both ALLOW both escape rows. #1213 neither causes nor fixes this, and it does fix the paren-in-string case that was live when I first measured it — so #1213 is a strict improvement and I have left its auto-merge armed.

One incidental difference, no behavioural cost: main BLOCKs `echo $(echo "x) > <protected>` and #1213's head ALLOWs it. Both are rc=2 syntax errors, so neither decision reaches a real write.

## Fix direction

Make the substitution scanner a character walk that honours `\` and the single/double-quote asymmetry (single quotes take no escapes; `\"` escapes inside double quotes), rather than `indexOf`.

**Do not reach for the fail-closed-on-unterminated change in the same commit.** It is the tempting addition and the measurement above says it buys nothing: the only spellings that reach that branch do not run. Shipping it alongside the real fix would make the regression test green for two reasons and leave nobody able to say which one held.

Acceptance rows, both expected red first:

- `echo $(echo "x\"") > <protected>` → BLOCK
- `echo $(echo "a\")b") > <protected>` → BLOCK
- and keep the five blocking controls above, or the battery cannot show the fix did anything.

Worth sweeping the corpus for real incidence as #1203/#1205 were — both of those measured 0, and a verb list built from the histogram was worth more than the filed shapes.

SUCCESS.md claim moved: 3 — the harness's own checks are able to fail. This one cannot, today, against a command that runs.
title: Write-guard bypass: an escaped quote inside $( ) swallows the redirect operator — ALLOWed, and the executed command overwrote the file
